extracted.intended_audience: UAI 2015 reviewers / program committee members (academic conference reviewers in machine learning/probabilistic inference)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing reviews and scoring submissions to the UAI 2015 conference: what reviewers should write (summary, strengths/weaknesses) and how to score papers on multiple dimensions using a 7-point scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Your review should address both the strengths and weaknesses of the paper - identify the areas where you believe the paper is particularly strong and particularly weak - this will be very valuable to the program chairs and the SPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about strong points and weak points; these are valuable to chairs and the Senior Program Committee when making decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain in your own words what is the problem that the paper is trying to address, and by what approach. In what area lie the main accomplishments of the paper. Optionally, a summary of your opinion, impact and significance could be included too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise, clear summary so chairs and readers understand the paper's goals and contributions. Use this section to demonstrate you understood the submission before critiquing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is arguably the single most important criterion for selecting papers for the conference. Reviewers should reward papers that propose genuinely new ideas, papers that truly depart from the 'natural' next step in a given problem or application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty relative to the problem/application area; do not infer novelty for the authors—authors should state what is novel. Determine whether ideas are truly new or are novel combinations/adaptations/extensions of existing ideas. Recognize novelty can be subjective and relative; justify your judgment with references when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results technically sound? Are there obvious flaws in the conceptual approach? Are claims well-supported by theoretical analysis or experimental results? Did the authors ignore (or appear unaware of) highly relevant prior work? Are the experiments well thought out and convincing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for conceptual flaws, adequacy of theoretical/experimental support, consideration of prior work, presence of obvious missing experiments. Consider replicability: will others be able to replicate results? Are data sets and/or code publicly available? Is the evaluation appropriate? Did authors discuss sensitivity to parameter settings? Point out specific missing analyses or experiments and suggest improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential Impact and Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this really a significant advance in the state of the art? Is this a paper that people are likely to read and cite in later years? Does the paper address an important problem? Does it raise new research issues for the community? Is it likely to have lasting impact or be useful 5–10 years from now?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both short-term and long-term influence, whether the work can be built on by others, and whether it addresses problems recognized beyond the immediate UAI community. Explain why you think the paper will (or will not) have impact, with concrete reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper clearly written? Does it adequately inform the reader? Is there a good use of examples and figures? Is it well organized? Are there problems with style and grammar? Are there issues with typos, formatting, references, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the full range of scores to identify poorly-written papers. Authors are responsible for writing clearly; reviewers should not be expected to extract information from poorly written manuscripts. Because accepted papers have little time for fixes, consider advising authors to revise and resubmit rather than accept a poorly written version. If the paper is likely to be accepted, give concrete suggestions to improve clarity and list specific typos or formatting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Comments to the Authors (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional section to add additional comments for the authors that don’t naturally fit into any of the sections above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this for detailed suggestions, clarifications, or points that would otherwise clutter other sections. Keep tone constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential Comments to SPC and Program Chairs (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional section for comments you would like to communicate to the SPC and program chairs, but that you do not wish to be seen by the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate uses include rankings or comparisons among the papers you have reviewed, or other candid recommendations for chairs. Do not include material you want authors to see here.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Advice on Review Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as precise as you can in your comments to the authors and avoid vague statements. Your criticism should be constructive where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If giving a low score, explain actions authors could take to improve the paper. Cite specific relevant prior work if claiming the paper is incremental. If experiments are unrealistic or insufficient, advise what could improve them (e.g., more realistic datasets, larger datasets, different evaluation metrics, sensitivity analyses). Avoid vague criticisms; give concrete, actionable feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric Scoring: 7-point overall recommendation scale
rubrics_metrics.description: A 7-point scoring system for overall recommendation: 7 = excellent (very strong acceptance; will fight for acceptance, potential best-paper); 6 = very good (should be accepted); 5 = good (accept if possible); 4 = decent but may be below threshold (tend to vote reject); 3 = weak (vote reject but could be persuaded otherwise); 2 = clear rejection; 1 = strong rejection (surprised it was submitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strongly encourage use of full range of scores and avoid clustering in the middle. New reviewers should calibrate using recent proceedings. The numeric score complements, but does not replace, the in-depth textual review. Additionally, you will score Novelty, Technical Quality, Significance, and Writing numerically: scores of 5 and higher mean the paper is at the standard for an accepted paper at UAI; 4 means weak in that area but possibly fixable before publication; scores below 4 mark serious flaws.
